briefing.specialist: A major dust storm arrives around sol 8, cutting solar power sharply for about two and a half days.
briefing.cadet: Around day 8, a huge dust storm will block the sun for a couple of days.

briefing.specialist: A solar particle event arrives early, around day 4 — the crew will need to shelter.
briefing.cadet: Around day 4, a solar storm means everyone has to hide in the safe room.

briefing.specialist: A solar particle event arrives partway through the first lunar night, around day 6.
briefing.cadet: Around day 6, deep in the first long night, a solar storm hits.

briefing.specialist: A 14-day lunar agricultural evaluation. Balance greenhouse power against survival needs to bring two crop trays to harvest.
briefing.cadet: Grow fresh plants on the Moon for 14 days. Save battery power when it gets dark.

briefing.specialist: Replays the May 10, 2024 solar storm from NASA DONKI records (based on real solar activity). Intense proton flux begins at hour 13 with 73-minute onset warning — prepare the shelter and manage battery power.
briefing.cadet: A big solar storm hits at day 1 (based on real solar activity). Move everyone inside the storm shelter.

briefing.title: Mission Briefing

partial.specialist: The mission can end with the whole crew alive but the goal unmet — a real, distinct outcome from a crew loss, not a milder version of it.
partial.cadet: Everyone can make it home safe, but still not finish the mission's goal.

abort.specialist: The crew can end the mission early, on purpose, if things are going badly enough — a real, deliberate call, not a failure of skill.
abort.cadet: You can decide to end the mission early to keep everyone safe.

loss.specialist: If every crew member is lost, the mission ends immediately, whatever else was going right.
loss.cadet: If the whole crew is lost, the mission is over.

briefing.massLine: {{kg}} kg of hardware, packed with real PDR-phase margin (NASA Ames APR 8070.1) — see the full breakdown on Mission Command.
briefing.massLineCadet: The ship is packing about {{kg}} kg of gear.

solSummary.quiet: A quiet sol — nothing significant to report.
solSummary.quietCadet: A quiet day — nothing big happened.

briefing.specialist: Translunar return trajectory. LiOH canisters are incompatible — cabin ppCO₂ is climbing steadily toward toxic levels. Improvise a scrubber adapter before lethal hypercapnia occurs.
briefing.cadet: On the way back from the Moon, carbon dioxide is building up in the air. Build the filter fix before the air gets dangerous.

briefing.specialist: Historical August 1972 solar particle event. Unshielded surface dose rates exceed acute radiation sickness thresholds — evacuate EVA crew to the regolith storm shelter immediately.
briefing.cadet: A giant solar storm hits the Moon. Send everyone outside into the storm shelter right away.

briefing.specialist: Kvant-1 oxygen generator fire. Toxic smoke and flames threaten module integrity and escape routes — deploy extinguishers and isolate ventilation immediately.
briefing.cadet: A fire started in an oxygen maker on Mir. Put on masks, fight the fire, and stop the smoke from spreading.

firstLight.idea: A base can only use power it has made or saved. The Moon's night lasts about 15 days.
firstLight.detail: The night lasts {nightHours} hours. The battery must cover the whole load, so the lowest-priority loads are turned off first.
firstLight.question: Why does the crew turn off the garden lights before the long night?

options.A: Plants grow better in the dark.
options.B: To save battery power for air and heat.

firstLight.rightFeedback: Right! The battery holds only so much power. The crew needs it for air and heat first.
firstLight.wrongFeedback: Not quite. The night lasts about 15 days. The battery must last the whole time, so the crew saves power for air and heat.

stormWarning.idea: Thick walls help keep people safe from radiation. But hiding costs time and power.
stormWarning.detail: Shielding thickness (g/cm²) cuts radiation dose. Sheltering costs crew-hours and pauses science and outside work.
stormWarning.question: The crew waits in the storm shelter for many hours. What do they give up?

options.A: Time for outside work and science.

stormWarning.rightFeedback: Right! Every hour in the shelter is an hour not spent working. Staying safe has a price.
stormWarning.wrongFeedback: Not quite. In the shelter the crew is safe, but they can't do outside work or science. Staying safe has a price.

greenThumb.idea: Plants need light to grow. In space, lamps make that light, and lamps use power.
greenThumb.detail: The greenhouse lights draw {greenhouseKw} kW in this mission. Fewer lit hours means slower growth and less food.
greenThumb.question: The crew turns the garden lights down to save power. What happens to the plants?

options.A: They grow faster in the dark.
options.C: They grow more slowly, so there is less food later.

greenThumb.rightFeedback: Right! Less light means slower growth. Saving power can cost food later.
greenThumb.wrongFeedback: Not quite. Plants use light to grow. With less light they grow more slowly, so there is less food later.

helloEarth.idea: A message from Mars takes at least 3 minutes to reach Earth. The crew often has to decide alone.
helloEarth.detail: One-way light-time is about {lightTimeMinMin} to {lightTimeMaxMin} minutes, depending on the Earth–Mars distance (JPL Horizons).
helloEarth.question: A fire alarm sounds on Mars. Should the crew wait for Earth's answer?

options.B: No. The answer would come too late, so the crew acts first.
options.C: Yes. Messages arrive in one second.

helloEarth.rightFeedback: Right! A message takes at least 3 minutes to get to Earth, and the answer takes as long to come back. For a fire, the crew must act first.
helloEarth.wrongFeedback: Not quite. A message from Mars takes at least 3 minutes to reach Earth. The answer takes as long to come back. For a fire, the crew must act first.
